source.title: Dynamic Short Convolutions Improve Transformers
source.authors: Oliver Sieberling; Bharat Runwal; Rameswar Panda; Yoon Kim

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out language-model validation loss across model scales and fits loss-versus-compute scaling curves, using a different architecture setting from the original studies.
record.gate_note: The scaling-law results in Section 3.2 and Appendix D bear on V1. The paper varies model size and training tokens together at an approximately fixed token-to-parameter ratio, so it does not isolate parameter-count or token-count scaling. Downstream evaluations, synthetic-task results, kernel benchmarks, and throughput measurements are not tests of downstream predictability or of the other claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper is about an architecture. It fits loss-vs-compute curves (C^-0.054) only to measure dynamic convolutions' compute advantage over Transformers. It never assesses whether loss follows a power law: no goodness of fit, no residuals, no check for deviation from the curve. It also does not test extrapolation, allocation or shape. The sweep is five sizes at a fixed ~50 token/parameter ratio, covering about 0.09–15 PFLOP-days (~2 orders of magnitude). Scaling laws are used as a measuring tool, not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that dynamic short convolutions consistently improve dense, MoE and linear-RNN language models over standard and static-convolution baselines. Fitted scaling curves give 1.33× (QKV) and 1.60× (all-linear) compute advantages. Custom Triton kernels keep end-to-end training slowdown modest: ~8% for QKV and 22–25% for all-linear. They caution that frontier-scale behaviour is not demonstrated.
record.recipe_differences: Fits held-out validation loss against training compute, but tests Transformers augmented with dynamic convolutions rather than the original scaling-law setups; model size and token count scale together at an approximately fixed ratio.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported compute advantage varies with dynamic-convolution placement (1.33× for Q/K/V and 1.60× for all linear layers). For the Q/K/V variant, it is 1.30×, 1.33×, or 1.34× under the Csimple, Cfull, and Cchinchilla compute conventions, respectively.

fits_no_version.finding: The compute advantage of the dynamic-convolution variant over Transformers barely changes with the FLOP-counting convention: 1.30×, 1.33× and 1.34× under Csimple, Cfull and Cchinchilla. The attention term accounts for 25–47% of Cfull.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Relative compute-advantage estimates between architectures are robust to the FLOP-counting convention.

record.peer_reviewed: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
record.problems: The scaling sweep covers 150M–2B dense models and does not establish the same trend at frontier scale. Model size and token count are varied together at an approximately fixed ratio, so their separate scaling relationships are not identified. The scaling curves are shown graphically without uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results were extracted. The paper's downstream task results are comparisons among trained models, not an analysis of downstream predictability with scale or pretraining loss.

untested.parts: Whether loss follows a power law: no fit-quality assessment. Parameter and token scaling are not separated (fixed ~50 tokens/param). Only ~2 orders of compute.
No extrapolation from small to larger runs.
No fixed-compute sweep of N/D allocation.
No depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count. The ablations vary convolution hyperparameters, not model shape.
No other modalities or regimes. MoE and linear-RNN results are single-scale.
Downstream accuracy is reported at a few scales but not analysed as a function of scale or loss.
Only the compute-advantage ratio is refit under different FLOP conventions. Exponents and allocations under different choices are not reported.

record.verdict_notes: The reader labelled this T1 'supports' for V1, but the scaling fits are an instrument for comparing architectures, not an examination of the scaling law. Even read generously, the evidence spans five points over ~2 orders of compute, with no fit-quality statistics. Fitted exponents are about -0.054 for both architectures; the study does not discuss them.

versions.untested_parts: Independent parameter-count and token-count scaling when the other factors are not bottlenecks; several-orders-of-magnitude evidence for those separate relationships.
No explicit test of whether fits from small runs predict substantially larger runs.
No sweep of parameter/token allocations at fixed compute and no compute-optimal allocation trend.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No tests of other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling laws.
Downstream evaluations are reported, but the study does not analyze or fit downstream performance as a predictable function of scale or pretraining loss.
The study checks compute-advantage robustness under alternative compute conventions, but does not test setup- or fitting-dependent exponents or compute-optimal splits.

rows.subject: Transformer scaling sweep (150M–2B)
rows.operation_detail: Fit validation loss against training compute across model scales.
rows.measure: Validation loss versus training compute; fitted scaling curve.
rows.note: The plotted fit is labeled 2.826 × C^-0.054. The curve covers five model sizes; individual plotted loss values are not stated numerically.
rows.check: Transformer fit (2.826 × C^-0.054) serves only as the baseline for the compute-advantage comparison. Fit quality and per-point losses are not reported. N and D are scaled together at a fixed ratio, over ~2 orders of compute. It cannot show whether a power law holds beyond being assumed.

rows.subject: Transformer with dynamic short convolutions on Q, K, and V (scaling sweep)
rows.operation_detail: Fit validation loss against training compute across model scales.
rows.measure: Validation loss versus training compute; fitted scaling curve.
rows.note: The plotted fit is labeled 2.778 × C^-0.054. The authors report an approximate 1.33× advantage over compute-matched Transformer baselines.
rows.check: This is the study's own method compared with a baseline (1.33× compute advantage). It is a performance claim for the new architecture, not a test of the power-law form.

rows.operation_detail: Fit validation loss against training compute across model scales.

rows.note: The plotted fits are labeled 2.826 × C^-0.054 for Transformer and 2.746 × C^-0.053 for the all-linear dynamic-convolution variant. The authors report a 1.60× advantage over compute-matched Transformer baselines.
rows.check: This is the study's own method compared with a baseline (1.60× advantage; fit 2.746 × C^-0.053). It is method performance, not a test of the scaling law.
